title: Very Strong Showing For Bonds Considering The Headwinds
summary:
Very Strong Showing For Bonds Considering The Headwinds 

             
             
            There were two major headwinds in play for the bond market today. Most obviously, the jobs report was very strong--something that would normally push rates logically and obviously higher. One can only run through a list of potential explanations to fit that paradoxical result (unemployment rate wasn't as far from forecasts, election impact still being weighed, tech stocks didn't bounce big, stale data if mid-October marked a shift in economic momentum) but mind you, no one would have pointed to these things as reasons for bonds to completely defy the jobs report if they had to guess at the impact ahead of time. The second headwind was the absence of additional selling in tech stocks. This one could go both ways. On on hand, the NASDAQ is higher than it was yesterday afternoon. On the other hand (and to reiterate a bullet point above) it didn't stage any sort of impressive recovery. The net effect for bonds was modest weakness although things would have been weaker were it not for mid-day news regarding Microsoft winding down a deal to rent AI cloud compute from Oracle.

title: Mortgage Rates Hold Steady at Lows Despite Stronger Jobs Report
summary:
Today was an odd one for mortgage rates. Anyone who's been following the rate market for very long will tell you that the monthly jobs report is one of the most reliable source of volatility for rates. In general, when job growth is much stronger than expected, rates rise and vice versa.  But in today's case, rates managed to hold perfectly flat despite the jobs report absolutely crushing expectations. Understand that no one who is offering a reason for this would have predicted this result if they knew the jobs numbers ahead of time and were simply asked to predict how rates would react. In other words, the only reason you're getting their explanations is because the paradoxical market reaction demanded a different narrative.  The only things that were true both before and after the jobs report were as follows:  
 The Fed recently said it was almost exclusively focused on the inflation side of its dual mandate (stable prices + maximum employment). 
 Bonds/rates have been preoccupied taking cues from concerns about the tech sector and heavy selling in tech stocks. 
 Bonds/rates/stocks are still in the process of making sense of this week's election results. 
 Markets have been more interested in the unemployment rate component of the jobs report than the payroll count (it was the latter that really surged in today's data).  
  None of these bullet points would have fully predicted the paradoxical resilience in rates today, but they perhaps help get us close to wrapping our minds around it. At the end of the day, the average lender was right in line with yesterday's levels--the lowest since September 22nd.   [thirtyyearmortgagerates]

title: Super Strong Jobs Report NOT Hitting Bonds Like You'd Expect
summary:
Nonfarm payrolls came in 100k higher than forecast and the unemployment dropped even as the participation rate moved higher. That's a recipe for a bond market sell-off if we ever saw one. But apart from an initial knee-jerk sell-off, yields returned back in line with pre-NFP levels within 8 minutes and haven't moved much since then. 
 What gives? Well... we expect that this is one of those days where market commentators are forced to adapt their narrative to the trading as opposed to hoping the trading would validate their narrative.  One caveat is that professional/biz services accounted for +70k of the 165k total, whereas it has averaged +15k over the past year. This isn't enough to discount the strength of the data. In fact, it's a genuinely strong report. Bonds simply don't care (apart from ultra short term bills and Fed Funds Futures). Neither did stocks for that matter. 
  
 In the interest of analytical authenticity, here are the only thoughts we would have shared even if bonds were selling off in response to this data (perhaps some of the resilience coincides with some of these to some extent, but if anyone tells you they saw this market reaction coming, yell at them and tell them to tell you ahead of time next time so you can both make some money trading). 
 
 Bonds were already 3+ bps weaker overnight 
 Fed recently and explicitly said it's focused on inflation side of mandate (mentioned yesterday as well) 
 Bonds have been primarily taking cues from AI deflation trade 
 Tech stocks moved modestly higher overnight, and bonds might not want to get carried away selling off if the tech rout might have an encore 
 Stocks/Bonds are also still trying to make sense of what election results might imply about the tech trade (and data center buildout pace, which could imply a downgraded view of corporate bond issuance, thus helping Treasuries/MBS).

title: Just 22% Of Homebuyers Are First-Timers As Cash Purchases Rise
summary: First-time homebuyers remain largely on the sidelines of the housing market, accounting for just 22% of purchases as older, equity-rich repeat buyers continue to dominate, according to new data from the National Association of Realtors (NAR).The first-time buyer share edged up from last year's record low of 21%, but remains far below the roughly 40% historical norm before the Great Recession. Meanwhile, the median age of first-time buyers held at a record 40, compared with 62 for repeat buyers.

title: Strong Jobs Report Threatens Mortgage Rate Rally
summary: Mortgage professionals hoping the recent rate rally had more room to run got some unwelcome news Friday.U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above the 65,000 economists expected, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2%.Bond traders reacted quickly. Treasury yields climbed following the report, putting pressure on a rally that had helped bring mortgage rates down for three consecutive weeks.
